articles.title: Price per credit is the wrong way to compare AI app builders
articles.excerpt: I spent the last few weeks reading pricing pages of AI app builders. Partly because I'm building one myself (builddu), partly because I kept getting confused. On paper it looks easy. Lovable Pro is $2…
articles.body: I spent the last few weeks reading pricing pages of AI app builders. Partly because I'm building one myself (builddu), partly because I kept getting confused. On paper it looks easy. Lovable Pro is $25 for 100 credits. Base44 Starter is $20 for 100 message credits. My own Starter plan is $20 for 100 credits. So they all cost about the same, right? Not really, because a credit means something different on every platform. Four ways to bill the same thing Lovable has one credit balance, plus some free grants for cloud and AI that get used first. Base44 splits it into two balances: message credits for building, and integration credits for what the finished app does. Bolt bills in tokens, so the cost depends on how much code and conversation the AI has to read each time.

articles.title: Integration tests for agent tools that run code: fixtures, cleanup, labels and budgets
articles.excerpt: Your agent's run_code tool is probably tested with a mock: call the tool, assert the mock was called with the right command, return a canned result. That test proves your code calls a function. It doe…
articles.body: Your agent's run_code tool is probably tested with a mock: call the tool, assert the mock was called with the right command, return a canned result. That test proves your code calls a function. It does not prove that pytest exists in the template, that a 200 KB output is truncated the way you think, that a timed-out command is reported as a timeout, or that the sandbox really cannot reach the internet. Those are the bugs that show up in production, as confused model behaviour that nobody can reproduce. A small integration suite against real sandboxes catches them. This post shows how to structure one with Vitest and the Sandscale TypeScript SDK; the approach carries over to any provider and test runner.

articles.title: European Accessibility Act in 2027: An Accessibility Guide for WooCommerce Stores
articles.excerpt: An online shopper should not have to abandon an order because the checkout cannot be operated with a keyboard, the error message is announced only by colour, or a payment window is inaccessible to a s…
articles.body: An online shopper should not have to abandon an order because the checkout cannot be operated with a keyboard, the error message is announced only by colour, or a payment window is inaccessible to a screen reader. This is a practical problem for ecommerce businesses and, for certain services, a legal one. The European Accessibility Act (EAA) started applying on 28 June 2025. In 2027 the question is no longer when the deadline will arrive, but which obligations apply and whether the complete customer journey actually works. This guide covers WordPress and WooCommerce stores, consumer sales into the EU, keyboard and screen-reader testing, payment integrations, exceptions and actionable remediation. It is technical and commercial guidance, not jurisdiction-specific legal advice.

articles.title: Your App Needs a Night Guard, Not Another Dashboard
articles.excerpt: After launch, nobody walks through your Android app anymore. Here's why a daily patrol on a different phone catches what monitoring tools miss. During your closed test, a dozen people walked through y…
articles.body: After launch, nobody walks through your Android app anymore. Here's why a daily patrol on a different phone catches what monitoring tools miss. During your closed test, a dozen people walked through your app on a dozen different phones. They tapped things, got lost, hit the bugs and told you about them. Then you launched, the testers left, and nobody walks through your app anymore. Your server monitor says everything is green. Your crash dashboard is quiet. And somewhere, on one particular phone, your app opens to a blank screen. You'll find out from a one-star review. Dashboards wait. Guards walk. Most monitoring tools sit and wait for something to go wrong: a crash report, a server timeout, an error spike.

articles.body: A paid WooCommerce order arrives, the warehouse packs the parcel, and the carrier collects it. Days later the store receives a payment dispute from someone who says they never authorised the purchase. Another store wakes up to hundreds of failed payments for a low-cost product. A third pays return-shipping costs for cash-on-delivery parcels nobody collects. These are different incidents, but each can consume profit before the merchant knows what went wrong. WooCommerce fraud prevention is not a single plugin or a CAPTCHA checkbox. A workable system combines checkout abuse controls, payment-provider risk decisions, order review, delivery evidence, dispute handling and monitoring for genuine customers blocked by mistake.

articles.body: Most of us treat classic literature like a checklist to conquer in high school or college and then never touch those books again. You power through the plot, underline a few quotes for a term paper, and move on to whatever else is new. The catch is that great books rarely reveal their most fascinating tricks on the first pass. When you already know the ending, your brain stops racing for answers and begins to notice the machinery holding all those mysteries and themes together. articles.excerpt: Your guide to December's full Cold Moon, from peak times to skywatching highlights.
articles.body: The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon)..

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 25, 1970: NASA's 'wingless' M2-F3 'lifting body' aircraft makes its 1st powered flight ahead of supersonic tests
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft. After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights. The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet.

articles.title: SpaceX Starship debris becomes art in Ashley Zelinskie's 'The Weight of Space' (video, photos)
articles.excerpt: Explore Ashley Zelinskie's 'The Weight of Space' Monuments in marble, Ejecta prints, Launch Sequence sculptures and interactive Crowded Sky at Heft Gallery in New York City.
articles.body: When a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan. 2025, pieces of its heat shield washed ashore. Some of that material now hangs on a gallery wall in New York City, embedded in artist Ashley Zelinskie's print of the very explosion it survived. Look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface. Some of Zelinskie's friends vacationing on the islands had come across pieces of heat-shield tile. "I think you might want these," Zelinskie recalled one friend telling her. She did. The Brooklyn-based artist ground the fragments into dust and worked them into the print. Ashley Zelinskie incorporated dust from recovered SpaceX Starship heat-shield tiles into this print of the vehicle breaking apart over Turks and Caicos.

articles.title: Green light for Starmind: SpaceX gets approval to deploy 1 million AI satellites
articles.excerpt: The FCC has given SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit, a move that could transform the landscape of the final frontier.
articles.body: Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years. The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit. "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval. AI has become central to SpaceX's business plans and identity over the past year or so. For example, the company has said that it's eyeing a "total addressable market" of $28.5 trillion over the long haul — and nearly $23 trillion of that is in "enterprise AI applications." Starmind is key to those lofty ambitions.
